Condition: alert, patient, intellectually humbled by the relic, and determined to preserve questions alongside evidence.

set.name: Sava
set.description: Location: subterranean Namaru archive and the southern-basin excavation site. Goal: protect the Aro from unknown relic hazards while ensuring that the Orpheus evidence is interpreted rigorously rather than sentimentally. Relationships: Eren’s skeptical collaborator; member of the research party accountable to the keeper of the quiet laws and the Aro archive. Knowledge: helped uncover Orpheus and has witnessed the damaged human recordings, including evidence of scientific achievement, coercive systems, and contradictory acts of protection and harm; understands that patience and technological sophistication do not prove gentleness. Possessions: scarred excavation tools, listening and environmental instruments, archive access, and field records. Condition: cautious, disciplined, skeptical of comforting interpretations, and increasingly affected by the human voices.
Aro researchers Eren, Sava, and their team discovered the returning Orpheus capsule beneath the roots of an ancient tree and transported it to the subterranean archive at Namaru.

The Aro recovered damaged human images, voices, mathematics, and recordings from Orpheus, including Mara’s claims that survival is not proof of virtue and that humanity knew more than it was willing to answer for.

The Aro reconstructed evidence that humanity combined extraordinary scientific knowledge with repeated fear-driven choices involving domination, coercion, denial, and selective ideas of protection, while marking their translations and chronology as uncertain.

Eren and the Aro researchers must interpret Mara’s surviving message without reducing humanity to either innocence or monstrosity, then create and launch an accountable archive of their own society’s achievements, harms, uncertainties, and obligations toward the vanished species.

chapters.name: An Answer Across the Dark
chapters.content:
## An Answer Across the Dark

The first disagreement began with the word confession.

It appeared in Eren’s preliminary report, entered cautiously between two uncertainty marks: *The recovered speaker may be confessing to collective wrongdoing.* Sava read the sentence in the review chamber and struck it from the tablet.

“Confession requires an audience authorized to receive it,” she said. “We have neither the language nor the history.”

“We have the repeated admission.”

“We have sounds we interpret as admission.”

Eren folded his hands beneath his chin. The chamber’s membranes displayed Mara’s face in fragments: one eye, a cheek illuminated by the pale light of a screen, the brief movement of her mouth before the recording dissolved into static. Behind the image, the Aro had placed their confidence bands, pale rings that widened around every uncertain translation.

“She says survival is not proof of virtue,” Eren said. “She says her people knew more than they were willing to answer for. Whatever the grammar, the direction is clear.”

“Clear enough to make us careless.”

The keeper of the quiet laws stood at the entrance, listening. Her name was Oru, though in the archive she was addressed by her office rather than her birth-name. She carried a bundle of root-fibre sheets, the old form used when a record was too important to be altered without witnesses.

“Perhaps the argument is not whether it is a confession,” she said. “Perhaps the argument is what we want the word to permit us to do.”

Sava looked toward her. “Explain.”

“If confession, then we may believe the dead have submitted themselves to judgment. If warning, we may believe they have given us an instruction. If manipulation, we may believe they are still trying to govern us.”

Eren watched Mara’s broken face. “And if it is all three?”

“Then it is like most speech made by frightened beings.”

The researchers sat with that. Outside the chamber, water moved through Namaru’s foundations. The sound was soft and regular, like breathing through a wall.

The Aro had begun by treating Orpheus as an artifact. Then as a damaged library. Then as evidence of an extinct intelligence. Now, increasingly, they treated it as an encounter. The distinction troubled them. An artifact could be measured. A library could be catalogued. An encounter demanded a response, and responses carried obligations that could not be solved by better instruments.

Some of the Aro rejected that demand.

Pell, who had laughed at the image of the stringed instrument and later apologized to no one, presented a competing interpretation before the full archive council. The human recordings, he argued, had been assembled to produce a particular emotional reaction in a distant listener. Images of flooded settlements and detained families were placed beside music, children, flowers, and scientific diagrams. The sequence was not history. It was persuasion.

“They selected their worst failures and their most beautiful gestures,” Pell said. “That is not a record. It is a designed moral atmosphere.”

“Every archive selects,” said Eren.

“Then every archive manipulates.”

“Not equally.”

Pell’s throat membranes tightened. “You are already defending her.”

“I am refusing to pretend that uncertainty makes all interpretations identical.”

The council chamber warmed by a fraction as the debate intensified. The Aro’s architects had designed public rooms to register conflict without amplifying it, but old habits survived architecture. Voices rose. Representatives from the river districts demanded that Orpheus be sealed until its influence on civic decisions could be studied. A group of young astronomers proposed broadcasting the entire reconstruction beyond Namaru, arguing that a species capable of crossing interstellar darkness had something to teach them, even if the lesson was caution.

Others asked the question that could not be dismissed as fear.

“What if the capsule is still active?”

The lattice was damaged, but not silent. Its surviving circuits produced minute changes in the archive’s local fields. No one had proven that these were more than decaying functions. No one had proven they were less. Sava had isolated the machine from every civic network and placed listening instruments around it. Even so, when the archive council met, she stood with one hand on the emergency seal.

“Do not call caution cowardice,” she told the astronomers. “The vanished makers built systems that predicted their populations and then used those predictions to confine them. They may have believed themselves practical. They may even have saved lives. We cannot know whether this object carries a gift, a trap, or only the residue of an experiment.”

“Yet we continue to listen,” Eren said.

“Because destroying evidence is also a choice.”

That sentence entered the record without revision.

For many cycles, the Aro studied Mara’s message in layers. They separated what she said from what surrounded her saying. They marked the testimonies of displaced families, workers, islanders, prisoners, and officials. They could not restore the names of all the speakers, but they preserved the gaps. They did not convert a woman’s grief into proof of an entire planet’s character. They did not let the grandeur of human mathematics excuse the suffering visible in the same archive.

Mara’s moral choice became more legible than her biography.

She had not claimed that her people were uniquely evil. She had not offered their survival as evidence that their decisions were correct. She had preserved contradictions: the guard who showed tenderness inside a system of detention; the worker proud of building clean energy while admitting the danger imposed on his body; the communities protected by policies that also erased their languages; the scientist who had accepted compromise and later stood before judgment.

The Aro understood contradictions. Their own history contained them, though their histories had been written by victorious councils and softened by the passage of generations.

Oru ordered a new project.

It would not be called a reply at first. The name suggested confidence. They called it the Near Archive: a record of the Aro as they were, not as they wished to be remembered.

Every district sent material. The river authorities submitted maps of the diversion debate, including their private projections and the names of villages that had been excluded from the first consultation. The nesting-keepers recorded the valleys their own expansion had damaged. The medical houses opened mortality ledgers long kept confidential, with families deciding which details could be public and which would remain within their care. The builders contributed designs that had failed during the southern quake. A former council speaker admitted that she had described a forced relocation as voluntary because the official word had seemed less painful.

They recorded achievements as well. The first deep-soil gardens. The repair of the moon-listening array. The cure for the ash fever. Songs composed during the famine years. The names of those who had shared water before the distribution laws changed.

No entry was allowed to stand alone.

Beside each success, the archive asked who had been excluded, who had paid, and what uncertainty remained. Beside each injustice, it asked who had resisted, who had tried to reduce the harm, and what conditions had made obedience appear reasonable. This was not an attempt to make every action equal. It was an attempt to keep moral weight from being hidden inside a single sentence.

Sava reviewed the first complete sequence in the listening vault. The Aro had chosen images, spoken testimony, mathematical notation, and periods of silence. They included the sound of the Namaru waterworks at night and the breathing of a child recovering from ash fever. They included a disagreement between two councils that had ended without a victor but with a revised plan.

“Will they understand us?” Eren asked.

“Who?”

“Whoever finds it.”

“Perhaps there will be no one.”

“Then why send it?”

Sava considered the question. The capsule’s damaged human voice was faint behind the sealed wall, a pulse beneath stone.

“Because the act changes us,” she said. “Not because it guarantees an audience.”

They built their vessel in the old orbital workshop, where the Aro’s first instruments had been shaped from metals drawn out of the deep crust. It was smaller than Orpheus and less ambitious. It carried no behavioral lattice, no hidden experiment, no mechanism designed to continue observing a population that had not consented. Its memory systems were redundant and legible. Every compression method was documented. Every access authority was named. A physical copy of the consent rules traveled inside it, along with instructions for destroying the archive without damaging a living world.

Before the launch, Eren asked that one final recording be made.

He sat before the listening membrane with Sava and Oru beside him. Behind them, the archive displayed a reconstruction of Earth: blue, clouded, and impossibly old. Mara’s face appeared in the corner, not as an icon but as one uncertain source among thousands.

Eren spoke slowly, allowing the translators to separate each phrase.

“To the vanished makers who called themselves human, if that name has been recovered correctly:

“We found your vessel beneath roots. We found your numbers, your songs, your machines, and the traces of the people your histories failed to keep. We do not know the whole of you. We will not turn fragments into a verdict.

“We found the warning. We remember the choice within it: to preserve failure without surrendering compassion, and to ask compassion without using it to erase responsibility.

“We have made an archive of ourselves. It contains what we built, what we broke, what we permitted, what we opposed, and what we still do not understand. It contains the names of those who benefited and those who were made to pay. If we have lied in it, we have marked where the lie may be found.

“You wanted the future to know that survival was not proof of virtue. We have learned that remembrance is not proof of wisdom either.

“If anyone hears us, let them judge carefully. If no one hears us, let the effort remain true.

“We found your warning. We remember your choice. We will try to deserve the chance to be remembered.”

For a moment no one moved.

Then the vessel rose through the forest.

Its engine disturbed the upper leaves, scattering luminous spores across the dark. Namaru’s people watched from terraces and listening wells as the small craft climbed beyond the weather, beyond the silver birds, beyond the atmosphere whose composition had changed many times since human hands first measured it.

The Aro had no certainty that it would reach another mind. They had no promise that the stars were inhabited, or that any future listener would be kinder than they had been. They sent it because certainty was not the condition of responsibility.

Far below, Orpheus continued its patient silence.

The two archives traveled in opposite directions through the dark: one carrying the record of a vanished species asking not to be absolved, the other carrying an answer that refused both condemnation and trust without evidence.

Between them lay eight million years, and all the distance still unmeasured.

The message went on.

set.name: Eren
set.description: Location: subterranean Namaru archive and the Aro orbital workshop, now overseeing the newly launched Near Archive and continued study of Orpheus. Goal: interpret the vanished makers’ evidence without turning uncertainty into a verdict, preserve questions alongside records, and help the Aro answer responsibly. Relationships: scientific collaborator and intellectual counterpart to Sava; works with keeper Oru and the wider archive council; regards Mara’s moral choice as more recoverable than her full biography. Knowledge: understands that Mara preserved evidence of human failure while retaining compassion, that human achievements and coercions were intertwined, and that the Aro’s own archive must record exclusions, benefits, harms, and uncertainties. Possessions: excavation instruments, translation records, archive tablets, confidence markings, access to the Orpheus chamber, and launch records for the Near Archive. Condition: alert, patient, intellectually humbled, and newly committed to responsibility without certainty after helping send the Aro’s answer into the dark.

set.name: Sava
set.description: Location: Namaru’s sealed listening vault and orbital launch facilities, monitoring Orpheus and the Aro archive’s outbound vessel. Goal: protect the Aro from unknown relic hazards while ensuring that both human evidence and Aro self-records are interpreted rigorously rather than sentimentally. Relationships: Eren’s skeptical collaborator; works with keeper Oru, the archive council, and research teams; respects Mara’s refusal to destroy evidence but distrusts comforting interpretations. Knowledge: knows Orpheus may be a damaged library, warning, manipulation, or residue of an experiment; understands that caution is not cowardice and that the Aro’s own archive must name who benefited and who paid. Possessions: scarred excavation tools, listening and environmental instruments, emergency seal authority, field records, and launch verification logs. Condition: cautious, disciplined, and emotionally affected by the human voices, yet willing to accept the obligations created by listening.

set.name: Oru
set.description: Location: subterranean Namaru archive and the Aro council chambers, responsible for the principles governing Orpheus interpretation and the Near Archive. Goal: ensure that records remain accountable, uncertainty is marked, and the Aro do not use the vanished makers’ history to flatter or condemn themselves without examination. Relationships: keeper of the quiet laws; works with Eren, Sava, archive councils, affected districts, and community reviewers. Knowledge: understands that calling Mara’s message confession, warning, or manipulation each creates different permissions for the living; knows the Aro have recorded their own achievements, injustices, exclusions, and unresolved questions before sending an answer toward the stars. Possessions: root-fibre witness sheets, archive authority, consent rules, revision protocols, and the final launch record. Condition: measured, ethically demanding, and protective of both evidence and living communities, accepting that responsibility does not require certainty or an audience.
The Aro council debated whether Mara’s surviving message was confession, warning, or manipulation, and recorded the principle that destroying uncertain evidence is also a choice.
The Aro created the Near Archive, documenting their achievements, injustices, uncertainties, and obligations with source context, exclusions, and revision marks rather than a simplified account.
Eren, Sava, and keeper Oru launched the Aro’s accountable archive toward the stars with a message to humanity promising to remember the warning and try to deserve remembrance.

Julian Vey did not resign. He disappeared.
The tribunal had been announced that morning by a coalition of states that did not agree on much except that the launch had made secrecy impossible.

At the far side of the crowd, Mara noticed men she did not recognize. They wore no university colors and carried signs printed with professional lettering: OPEN THE ARCHIVE, END THE COVER-UP. One of them had a coil of chain looped beneath his jacket.
